newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian doctor warns of euthanasia rush.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian doctor warns of euthanasia rush.

text.p: A leading Australian euthanasia campaigner warned on Tuesday that some terminally ill patients could panic and rush to use the world's first voluntary euthanasia law as Australian politicians try to overturn it.
Doctor Philip Nitschke, dubbed "Doctor Death" by critics, said several terminally-ill patients were seeking approval to use the assisted suicide law, fearful it would soon be quashed.

"People are feeling they want to act quickly because they see there's a window of opportunity and it's about to be slammed shut," said Nitschke, who helped a patient in September become the first to die using the law.
Australia's parliament on Monday began debating a bill to overturn the law, which took effect in the remote Northern Territory in July.
The national parliament has the power to overturn laws in Australia's two territories, but not the six states.
Parliament's lower house, the House of Representatives, is expected to support a private members bill which would see Canberra use its constitutional powers to axe the territory law.
The move by government backbencher Kevin Andrews has the support of Prime Minister John Howard. Labor opposition leader Kim Beazley has also publicly opposed the territory's law.
Australia's main political parties are allowing members a conscience vote on the issue, freeing them from party policy.
"It does not look good -- I feel a bit pessimistic about it," Nitschke told Reuters by telephone from the territory's capital Darwin. "(But) hopefully, some common sense and sanity might intervene."

The anti-euthanasia bill must still face the Australian parliament's upper house Senate, where its fate is less certain. The law is also being challenged in the High Court by a coalition of doctors, church and Aboriginal leaders.
Although the law came into operation in July, legal and political wrangles delayed its use until last month, when cancer patient Bob Dent became the first to die using the law.
Dent's son, Rod, on Monday made a impassioned plea to national politicians not to overturn the law.

"I make a plea from my heart to all federal politicians on behalf of my father and all dying patients who want the right to choose voluntary euthanasia if their suffering becomes too great," Rod Dent said in a statement.
Nitschke said about 10 people had sought his help in obtaining approval for assisted suicide, with half approaching him in recent days amid fears the law may be overturned.
The law allows terminally-ill people who meet strict guidelines to kill themselves with a lethal injection or pills.
Doctors are allowed to help the patient commit suicide.
The controversial law has sparked an emotional debate in Australia, drawing criticism from civil leaders, church groups and the main doctors' body, the Australian Medical Association.
But opinion polls show an overwhelming majority of Australians -- about 75 percent -- support voluntary euthanasia.
